questions.prompt: In words, what does \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\) mean?
questions.answer:
It means \(f(x)\) can be made as close as desired to \(L\) by taking \(x\) sufficiently close to \(a\), with \(x\ne a\).
The value of \(f(a)\) itself is not the main issue; the nearby behavior is.

questions.prompt: In the epsilon-delta definition, which quantity is chosen first: \(\epsilon\) or \(\delta\)?
questions.answer:
\(\epsilon\) is chosen first.
The definition says that for every \(\epsilon>0\), there must exist a \(\delta>0\) such that
\[0<|x-a|<\delta\implies |f(x)-L|<\epsilon.\]

questions.prompt: Translate \(|f(x)-L|<\epsilon\) into interval notation for \(f(x)\).
questions.answer:
The inequality means \(f(x)\) is within \(\epsilon\) of \(L\).
So
\[-\epsilon<f(x)-L<\epsilon.\]
Add \(L\) throughout:
\[L-\epsilon<f(x)<L+\epsilon.\]

questions.prompt: Translate \(0<|x-a|<\delta\) into a statement about \(x\).
questions.answer:
The inequality \(|x-a|<\delta\) means
\[a-\delta<x<a+\delta.\]
The extra condition \(0<|x-a|\) means \(x\ne a\).
So \(x\) is inside the deleted interval around \(a\): close to \(a\), but not equal to \(a\).

questions.prompt: Use the epsilon-delta definition to prove \(\lim_{x\to2}(x+3)=5\).
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). We need \(|(x+3)-5|<\epsilon\).
Simplify:
\[|(x+3)-5|=|x-2|.\]
Choose \(\delta=\epsilon\). Then if \(0<|x-2|<\delta\),
\[|(x+3)-5|=|x-2|<\delta=\epsilon.\]
Therefore the limit is \(5\).

questions.prompt: Use the epsilon-delta definition to prove \(\lim_{x\to1}2x=2\).
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). We want \(|2x-2|<\epsilon\).
Factor:
\[|2x-2|=2|x-1|.\]
Choose \(\delta=\frac\epsilon2\). If \(0<|x-1|<\delta\), then
\[|2x-2|=2|x-1|<2\delta=\epsilon.\]
Thus \(\lim_{x\to1}2x=2\).

questions.prompt: Find a suitable \(\delta\) in terms of \(\epsilon\) to prove \(\lim_{x\to4}(3x-1)=11\).
questions.answer:
We need
\[|(3x-1)-11|<\epsilon.\]
Simplify:
\[|(3x-1)-11|=|3x-12|=3|x-4|.\]
To make this less than \(\epsilon\), require \(|x-4|<\frac\epsilon3\).
A suitable choice is
\[\delta=\frac\epsilon3.\]

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=5-2x\), find \(\delta\) in terms of \(\epsilon\) to prove \(\lim_{x\to1}f(x)=3\).
questions.answer:
Compute the output error:
\[|f(x)-3|=|(5-2x)-3|=|2-2x|=2|x-1|.\]
To force \(2|x-1|<\epsilon\), require
\[|x-1|<\frac\epsilon2.\]
So choose \(\delta=\frac\epsilon2\).

questions.prompt: Prove \(\lim_{x\to3}(4x+1)=13\) using epsilon-delta language.
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). Choose \(\delta=\frac\epsilon4\).
If \(0<|x-3|<\delta\), then
\[|(4x+1)-13|=|4x-12|=4|x-3|<4\delta=\epsilon.\]
Therefore, by the epsilon-delta definition, \(\lim_{x\to3}(4x+1)=13\).

questions.prompt: Prove \(\lim_{x\to-2}(7-x)=9\) using epsilon-delta language.
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). We have
\[|(7-x)-9|=|-x-2|=|x+2|.\]
Choose \(\delta=\epsilon\). If \(0<|x-(-2)|=|x+2|<\delta\), then
\[|(7-x)-9|=|x+2|<\epsilon.\]
So the limit is \(9\).

questions.prompt: Explain why the condition \(0<|x-a|\) appears in the formal limit definition.
questions.answer:
The condition \(0<|x-a|\) excludes \(x=a\).
Limits describe what happens as \(x\) approaches \(a\), not necessarily what happens at \(a\).
This allows a limit to exist even if \(f(a)\) is undefined or different from the limiting value.

questions.prompt: A function satisfies \(f(x)=2x+1\) for \(x\ne1\), but \(f(1)=100\). What is \(\lim_{x\to1}f(x)\), and why?
questions.answer:
For \(x\ne1\), the nearby values are controlled by \(2x+1\).
So
\[\lim_{x\to1}f(x)=\lim_{x\to1}(2x+1)=3.\]
The value \(f(1)=100\) does not affect the limit because the formal definition uses \(0<|x-1|\).

questions.prompt: Prove \(\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4\) by first restricting \(|x-2|<1\).
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). We need
\[|x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|<\epsilon.\]
If \(|x-2|<1\), then \(1<x<3\), so \(3<x+2<5\), hence \(|x+2|<5\).
Choose
\[\delta=\min\left(1,\frac\epsilon5\right).\]
Then \(|x^2-4|<5|x-2|<5\delta\le\epsilon\).

questions.prompt: Prove \(\lim_{x\to1}x^2=1\) using an epsilon-delta argument.
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). Factor the error:
\[|x^2-1|=|x-1||x+1|.\]
If \(|x-1|<1\), then \(0<x<2\), so \(|x+1|<3\).
Choose
\[\delta=\min\left(1,\frac\epsilon3\right).\]
If \(0<|x-1|<\delta\), then
\[|x^2-1|<3|x-1|<3\delta\le\epsilon.\]

questions.prompt: Find a \(\delta\) that works for \(\lim_{x\to0}x^2=0\).
questions.answer:
We need \(|x^2-0|<\epsilon\), or \(|x|^2<\epsilon\).
This is guaranteed if
\[|x|<\sqrt\epsilon.\]
So choose
\[\delta=\sqrt\epsilon.\]
Then \(0<|x|<\delta\) implies \(|x^2|<\epsilon\).

questions.prompt: For \(\lim_{x\to a}cx=ca\), where \(c\ne0\), find a suitable \(\delta\) in terms of \(\epsilon\).
questions.answer:
The output error is
\[|cx-ca|=|c||x-a|.\]
To make this less than \(\epsilon\), require
\[|x-a|<\frac\epsilon{|c|}.\]
So a suitable choice is
\[\delta=\frac\epsilon{|c|}.\]

questions.prompt: A proof chooses \(\delta=\epsilon^2\) to prove \(\lim_{x\to0}x=0\). Does it work for every \(\epsilon>0\)? Explain.
questions.answer:
We need \(|x|<\epsilon\). If \(0<\epsilon<1\), then \(\epsilon^2<\epsilon\), so \(|x|<\epsilon^2\) works.
But if \(\epsilon>1\), then \(\epsilon^2>\epsilon\), so \(|x|<\epsilon^2\) does not guarantee \(|x|<\epsilon\).
A safe choice would be \(\delta=\min(1,\epsilon)\) or simply \(\delta=\epsilon\).

questions.prompt: Disprove the claim \(\lim_{x\to0}1=2\) using the epsilon-delta definition.
questions.answer:
Choose \(\epsilon=\frac12\).
For every \(x\),
\[|1-2|=1.\]
But \(1\not<\frac12\).
So no matter what \(\delta>0\) is chosen, the implication
\[0<|x-0|<\delta\implies |1-2|<\frac12\]
fails. Therefore the limit is not \(2\).

questions.prompt: Explain why the order \(\forall\epsilon>0\,\exists\delta>0\) cannot be swapped in the formal definition of a limit.
questions.answer:
The limit definition must work for every requested output tolerance \(\epsilon\). The allowed input distance \(\delta\) may need to shrink when \(\epsilon\) shrinks.
If the order were swapped, one fixed \(\delta\) would have to work before knowing how small \(\epsilon\) is. That would not express arbitrary closeness.
The correct order captures: first choose the demanded accuracy, then choose a close enough input window.

questions.prompt: Prove \(\lim_{x\to a}(mx+b)=ma+b\) for constant \(m\ne0\).
questions.answer:
Let \(\epsilon>0\). The output error is
\[|(mx+b)-(ma+b)|=|m(x-a)|=|m||x-a|.\]
Choose
\[\delta=\frac\epsilon{|m|}.\]
If \(0<|x-a|<\delta\), then
\[|(mx+b)-(ma+b)|=|m||x-a|<|m|\delta=\epsilon.\]
Therefore \(\lim_{x\to a}(mx+b)=ma+b\).
